summary: Scarcity forces choice, and each choice costs its best alternative; the PPF illustrates trade-offs and growth.
Micro studies individual markets and decision-makers; macro studies aggregates; policy pursues several goals with fiscal, monetary and trade instruments.
Demand and supply determine price and quantity; shifts, controls and taxes can be analysed with equations.

summary: Elasticity measures responsiveness; price elasticity is classified from perfectly inelastic to perfectly elastic and depends on substitutes, necessity, income share and time.
Total outlay, point and arc methods measure it; income and cross elasticities classify goods and relationships.
Elasticity guides pricing, taxation and policy.

summary: Cardinal analysis explains demand through diminishing marginal utility and the equi-marginal principle.
Ordinal analysis uses indifference curves and the budget line; equilibrium is tangency (MRS = price ratio).
Price effects decompose into substitution and income effects; PCC gives demand and ICC gives Engel curves.

summary: Economic cost includes implicit costs, so economic profit is lower than accounting profit; normal profit is a cost.
Short-run cost curves are U-shaped because of diminishing returns; long-run curves are envelopes shaped by scale economies.
Revenue curves are horizontal under perfect competition and downward-sloping with MR below AR otherwise.

summary: Every firm maximises profit where MR = MC; the market structure fixes the shape of MR.
Competition drives price to the minimum of average cost; monopoly restricts output and raises price, creating deadweight loss; price discrimination raises monopoly profit.
Monopolistic competition gives variety with excess capacity; oligopolists are interdependent and may collude but are tempted to cheat.

summary: The circular flow links output, income and spending; equilibrium needs leakages = injections.
GDP, GNP, NDP, NNP, NI, PI, DI and PCI are successive adjustments for foreign income, depreciation, taxes and transfers.
Real GDP strips out price changes using the deflator; national income is computed by product, income or expenditure methods, which agree.

summary: Money serves four functions; its value falls as the price level rises; the money supply (M1, M2) is created by banks via the multiplier and controlled by the central bank.
Inflation, caused by demand, costs or structure, redistributes income and is fought with monetary, fiscal and supply measures.
Commercial banks take deposits and lend; the NRB issues currency, regulates banks and conducts monetary policy.
International trade differs from domestic trade by frictions and currencies; BoT covers goods, while the BoP records all transactions and balances in total.
